Who benefits

  • Farmers: a free crop plan for every field, even keeping the crops they want (15–35 % less well water).
  • Cooperatives and water authorities: plan every field above one aquifer together.
  • Communities: wells last longer and the ground stays stable.

Why it works in the real world

  • Runs on free global data: NASA POWER weather and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate models.
  • Works in any browser. No sensors, no new hardware.
  • Follows local rules (Konya's 2027 plan). A new region needs only 3 inputs.

How we prove and scale it

  • Measure: well water per decare against today's rotation.
  • Pilot with farmers in Çumra, Konya, then verify savings with smart well meters.
  • Konya alone has about 160,000 wells (≈40,000 licensed, ≈120,000 unlicensed).

Wells: Reuters, Dec 2025 (Prof. Fetullah Arık, Konya Technical University). Savings: FieldRota-AI tests on unseen data.

Rare, extreme summers are where our model still struggles.

Autumn 2024: the AI chooses vetch for 2025
It cannot know next summer's heat
Usual July:0–3 hot days
July 2025:about 13 hot days
July is when vetch is most sensitive to heat. 2025 became the worst year of our test.
Hot day: 35 °C or higher

How we fix it

Add NASA seasonal forecasts (GEOS-S2S), which warn of heat months ahead.

Plus more data and more training.

Data: NASA POWER daily weather, Çumra, 1985–2025. Forecasts: NASA GMAO GEOS-S2S.

Next: four upgrades to the agent

changes the stateSeasonal forecasts

Add NASA's GEOS-S2S seasonal forecast to the state, so the agent sees a hot summer coming before it picks a heat-sensitive crop (the 2025 case).

changes the scaleWhole-aquifer planning

Plan every field above one aquifer together, so the total pumped stays within what rain gives back.

changes the inputField history from satellites

Read each field's past crops from NASA Landsat/HLS imagery, so nothing is typed by hand and real impact can be measured field by field.

changes the rewardMore than water

Add soil nitrogen balance, sunlight and expected yield to the reward; the farmer weighs the goals.
